lead: Thermodynamics studies energy, matter and their changes. You can follow every molecule, or you can measure bulk quantities. The microscopic view tracks molecules and uses statistics. The macroscopic view uses pressure p, volume V and temperature T that you can measure. Engineering uses the macroscopic view because a small sample holds an enormous number of molecules. Averages describe the sample well. The two views agree, and the bulk view is the practical one for design.
prereq: You need: school physics ideas of force, energy and density; systems and properties are defined next.

blocks.text: Thermodynamics is the study of energy, matter and the changes they undergo. It covers engines, refrigerators, steam plants, air conditioners and chemical reactions. Two points of view describe the same sample. The microscopic view follows individual molecules: where each one is, how fast it moves and how it collides. The macroscopic view ignores individual molecules and uses bulk properties that you can measure, such as pressure p, volume V and temperature T. Some syllabi call these the microscopic and macroscopic approaches. They are not rival theories. The microscopic model explains why the bulk properties behave as they do. The macroscopic model gives numbers you can use in design. Engineering calculations normally start from the macroscopic view and use the microscopic view only when a deeper reason is needed. The same copper block can be described by its mass, volume and temperature, or by the motion of its atoms. The first description is what an engineer measures. The second explains why the measurements follow the laws they do.

The microscopic view treats a sample as a very large number of molecules. A cubic centimetre of gas near room conditions holds about 10¹⁹ molecules. Tracking each molecule by hand is impossible. The method records molecular positions, speeds and collisions, then uses statistics to find averages. These averages predict bulk behaviour. For example, molecules strike the wall and transfer momentum; the average rate of momentum transfer per unit area is what we measure as pressure. Higher temperature means higher average molecular kinetic energy, so molecules hit harder and pressure rises if volume is fixed. Molecular kinetic theory and statistical mechanics build these links in detail; Unit 5 uses their results for gases. The microscopic view is powerful for explaining temperature, pressure and phase change. It is not convenient for routine calculations because the number of molecules is enormous and the detailed motion is not needed. The microscopic view does not replace measurements. It supplies a model that predicts what a gauge or thermometer will show. In a gas, the model treats collisions as random; in a solid, it treats atoms as vibrating about fixed positions. Both cases use averages, not individual fates.

The macroscopic view treats the whole sample as a continuous body with measurable properties. Pressure p is normal force per unit area: p = F / A, where p is pressure in pascal (Pa), F is normal force in newton (N), and A is area in square metre (m²). Volume V is the space occupied, in cubic metre (m³). Temperature T is the property that decides thermal equilibrium; the zeroth law defines it. Density ρ is mass per unit volume: ρ = m / V, where m is mass in kilogram (kg) and ρ is in kg/m³. A property measured for the whole sample, or for a uniform part of it, is macroscopic. The continuum idea assumes matter is continuous, so p, ρ and T vary smoothly from point to point. This works when the region of interest is much larger than molecular spacing, as in pipes, turbines and heat exchangers. It fails in a very thin gas layer near a surface. A property is macroscopic when it belongs to the sample or to a small continuum element, not to one molecule. Examples are p, V, T, density, internal energy and enthalpy. Internal energy and enthalpy are developed in Unit 2.

figure.caption: The tree separates the two views: tracking molecules with statistics, or using measured bulk properties p, V and T. Engineering calculations normally take the right branch.

spec.aria: A tree splits thermodynamic views into microscopic, which tracks molecules and uses statistics, and macroscopic, which uses measured bulk properties p, V and T.

examples.question: A copper block has mass 1.00 kg and volume 1.12×10⁻⁴ m³. Is density a microscopic or macroscopic property? Calculate its density.
steps: Density uses mass and volume of the whole block. Both are bulk measurements. So density is a macroscopic property.
Use the formula ρ = m / V, where ρ is density in kg/m³, m is mass in kg and V is volume in m³.
Substitute m = 1.00 kg and V = 1.12×10⁻⁴ m³.
Round to three significant figures: ρ ≈ 8.93×10³ kg/m³.
examples.answer: Density is a macroscopic property; its value is 8.93×10³ kg/m³ (8928.57 kg/m³).
examples.check:
mass = 1.00
volume = 1.12e-4
density = mass / volume
print(f'{density:.2f}')

traps: Pressure is not only microscopic. Molecular collisions explain it, but pressure is a bulk property measured with a gauge or transducer.
Density is not microscopic because copper contains atoms. Density uses total mass and total volume, so it is a macroscopic property.
Do not mix units: density from kg and m³ is kg/m³; from g and cm³ it is g/cm³. Convert before comparing.
The two views do not give different thermodynamics. They describe the same state; one follows molecules, the other measures averages.
The continuum is not valid at every scale. It fails when the flow region is comparable to molecular spacing or mean free path.

quiz.q: Define the microscopic approach in thermodynamics.
quiz.a: It tracks individual molecules, their positions, speeds and collisions, then uses statistics to predict average behaviour.

quiz.q: Why does engineering usually use the macroscopic view?
quiz.a: A sample has an enormous number of molecules, so tracking each is impractical; bulk properties p, V and T are measurable and enough for design.

quiz.q: A sample has mass 2.00 kg and volume 2.50×10⁻⁴ m³. Find density. Is it macroscopic?
quiz.a: ρ = m / V = 2.00 / (2.50×10⁻⁴) = 8000 kg/m³. It uses total mass and total volume, so it is macroscopic.

quiz.q: Pressure comes from molecular collisions. Explain why it is still called a macroscopic property.
quiz.a: The measured pressure is an average over very many collisions on a surface. A gauge reads this average bulk effect, not one molecule. So pressure is macroscopic even though its mechanism is molecular.

quiz.q: Name three macroscopic properties of a gas.
quiz.a: Pressure p, volume V and temperature T; density and mass also count.

quiz.q: What does the continuum idea assume?
quiz.a: Matter is treated as continuous, with properties such as p, ρ and T varying smoothly from point to point; molecular gaps are ignored.

quiz.q: A sensor measures average molecular speed in a tiny volume. A gauge measures pressure of the whole tank. Classify each as microscopic or macroscopic.
quiz.a: Average molecular speed in a tiny volume is a microscopic-type molecular quantity (statistical average). Tank pressure is a macroscopic bulk property.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern design uses both views: power-plant and HVAC engineers use macroscopic property tables, while CFD and materials researchers use microscopic models. Statistical mechanics connects them. Molecular dynamics simulates atoms; continuum solvers average the results. Search next: kinetic theory of gases, continuum mechanics, molecular dynamics.
